792.title: Caedmon's song
792.hook: a shy cowherd who hid when the harp came round dreams a song of creation
792.howItsDone: Christians in England remember Caedmon as a saint and as an early poet of English, and his story from Bede is often retold when churches talk about everyone having a voice in worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hilda, the abbess kings came to for advice. Your line was wisdom at whitby. What did she say when you asked? Day seven hundred ninety-two.

The harp is going round the table. It's a feast night, and the custom is that everyone takes a turn: the harp comes to you, you sing something, you pass it on. One man is watching it come closer, and his stomach is in knots. He can't sing. He has never been able to. So before it reaches him, he gets up, slips out the door, and walks off into the dark, the way he always does. It's his night to look after the cattle anyway. He goes to the stable, lies down near the animals, and falls asleep. Same as every feast. Except tonight, Bede says, someone is standing beside him in his sleep, calling him by name.
screen: `HE SLIPS OUT BEFORE IT REACHES HIM.`

segments.voice: His name is Caedmon, and he works for Hilda's monastery at Whitby, where we were yesterday. The voice in the dream says: Caedmon, sing me something. And he says what he always says: I can't sing. That's why I left the feast. The voice says: all the same, you will sing for me. Caedmon asks the only question left. What should I sing? Sing the beginning of created things. And he does. In the dream, Caedmon sings verses he has never heard before, praising God as the maker of heaven and earth. In the morning he still remembers them, and he can add more. He tells the man in charge of him, who takes him straight to Hilda. She calls in her learned people. They read him a passage of scripture and send him away, and the next morning he comes back with it turned into a poem. Hilda asks him to become a monk, and he spends the rest of his life turning the Bible's stories into songs in his own English. Bede tells us one more thing. He writes his history in Latin, so he gives Caedmon's song in Latin too. But he stops to say this is only the sense of it, not the words. A poem, Bede says, can't be carried from one language into another word for word without losing its beauty. So the shy man's song has to be heard in his own tongue. Bede adds that Caedmon learned the art of singing not from people but from God.

Here's the practice: sing something small. Nobody's listening, and nobody's grading. Settle, and breathe. Then let one short line of a song come out of you, as quietly as you like. A hymn you know, a lullaby, a line from the radio, or just a hum with no words. If singing feels impossible, that's exactly where Caedmon started; just hum one note and hold it. If you pray, the song can be your prayer. If you don't, let it simply be a sound you made on purpose. Then rest in the quiet after it. The bell holds the time.
Caedmon's song. The cowherd who walked out when the harp came round, and sang of creation in a dream.
Your line: even the shy sing. Today, hum or sing one line somewhere you usually wouldn't: in the car, in the kitchen, under your breath on the stairs. Day seven hundred ninety-two.

793.title: Cuthbert and the otters
793.hook: after praying all night in the sea, Cuthbert is warmed by otters
793.howItsDone: Christians in the north of England and the Scottish borders honor Saint Cuthbert, and pilgrims visit Lindisfarne, where he lived, and Durham Cathedral, where tradition places his shrine.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Caedmon's song, the shy cowherd who sang of creation. Your line was even the shy sing. Where did you hum? Day seven hundred ninety-three.

Somebody is following him. It's the middle of the night at a monastery by the sea, and a guest, a monk named Cuthbert, has slipped out while everyone sleeps. He does this, apparently. One of the brothers has noticed, and tonight curiosity wins. He creeps out after him, keeping his distance, down toward the shore. He expects, maybe, to catch the holy man doing something ordinary. Instead he watches Cuthbert walk straight into the sea, deeper and deeper, until the cold water is up around his neck. And there he stays. Today, what the brother saw, and what he did after.
screen: `INTO THE SEA, UP TO HIS NECK.`

segments.voice: The story comes from Bede, who wrote a life of Cuthbert. Cuthbert stands in the sea through the dark hours, Bede says, singing praises to God with the waves. When dawn comes he wades out and kneels on the sand to pray. And then two small animals come up out of the sea after him. They stretch out in front of him, warm his feet with their breath, and dry them with their fur. When they're done, Cuthbert blesses them, and they slip back into the water. The story is known today as Cuthbert and the otters. Then there's the brother watching from the shore. Bede says he's so shaken by what he's seen that he can barely walk home. In the morning he goes to Cuthbert and falls at his feet, in tears, asking forgiveness for spying. Cuthbert knows already. And he's gentle. He forgives him, on one condition: tell no one what you saw while I'm alive. The brother keeps the promise, and only after Cuthbert's death does the story come out. So there are two kindnesses in it. Animals caring for a man who was cold, and a man caring for a brother who was ashamed. Cuthbert later lived on Lindisfarne, the island Aidan came to from Iona a few days back in our story. Some readers see in the otters creation at peace with a holy person, like Adam among the animals in Eden. Others keep it simply as a story of two kindnesses on one cold shore.

Here's the practice: notice an animal's kindness. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind an animal that has been gentle with you or with someone you love. A dog that leans against your leg on a bad day. A cat that sits on the one person who's sad. A bird at the window. Even an animal you only watched once, caring for its young. Stay with that picture. Notice how it was given without words, and without asking anything back. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If you don't, just let yourself be warmed by the memory. The bell holds the time.
Cuthbert. A monk who stood in prayer in the cold sea at night, and whose feet two otters warmed at dawn, in a secret kept until he died.
Your line: the sea and the otters. Today, be warm to someone who's been out in the cold, and if you see a kindness, let it be theirs to tell. Day seven hundred ninety-three.

794.title: Bede
794.hook: a monk who wrote a history of the English church and died finishing a translation
794.howItsDone: Catholics and Anglicans honor the Venerable Bede as a saint, and Catholics count him a Doctor of the Church; his history is still read by students of the early English church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cuthbert, and a secret kept. Your line was the sea and the otters. Who did you warm up? Day seven hundred ninety-four.

"Dear master, there's still one sentence not written." A boy is sitting with a pen in a monk's cell in the north of England. On the floor nearby, an old monk is dying, and he's short of breath. They've been working all day. The old man has been dictating, the boy writing, and they are nearly done. All week, one man has stood behind the stories: Hilda, Caedmon, Cuthbert, Augustine and the temples. This dying monk wrote them down. His name is Bede. Today, the storyteller himself, and the last sentence.

Bede tells us a little about himself at the end of his history of the English church. He was given to the monastery as a child and spent his whole life there, at Wearmouth and Jarrow. His delight, he says, was always in learning, or teaching, or writing. He wrote in Latin, the language of scholars, and he wrote a great deal: on scripture, on time and the calendar, on the saints, and the history we've been reading from all week. His death comes to us in a letter from one of his students, a monk named Cuthbert, not the Cuthbert of the otters. In his last days, the letter says, Bede was translating the Gospel of John into English. He got as far as a verse in chapter six. A boy has a little food, and Andrew asks Jesus, "but what are they among so many?" He also stopped, the letter says, to hand out a few small things he owned, a little pepper, some cloth, some incense, to the priests of the house. Then the boy, Wilberht, says it. Dear master, one sentence left. Bede says: write it quickly. A moment later: it's finished. And Bede answers, you've spoken truly, it is finished. They are the words Jesus says from the cross in John's Gospel. Bede asks to be held, facing the place where he used to pray, and he dies on the floor of his cell, singing the old words of praise: glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. A whole life of work, and the last sentence still mattered.

Here's the practice: finish one sentence you started. Settle, and breathe. Think of something small you left half-done. An email sitting in drafts. A text you began and never sent. A thank-you note. A line in a journal. A sentence you started saying to someone and swallowed. Choose just one. If you can, finish it now, while the bell holds, and then put the pen or the phone down and breathe. If it has to wait, decide the exact words in your head. If you pray, you can offer the small work to God. If you don't, simply let it be done. The bell holds the time.
Bede. The monk of Jarrow who wrote the history we've been reading, and died translating John's Gospel, one sentence from the end.
Your line: finish the work. Today, send or say the sentence you finished. Then say to yourself, quietly, it is finished. Day seven hundred ninety-four.

795.title: Frumentius in Ethiopia
795.hook: a boy spared when his ship is attacked helps raise a prince, and comes back a bishop
795.howItsDone: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Christians honor Frumentius as Abba Salama, and their churches keep a tabot, a consecrated tablet, on the altar; at the feast of Timkat, the tabots are carried in procession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bede, who died one sentence from the end of his translation. Your line was finish the work. What did you finish? Day seven hundred ninety-five.

Two boys are sitting under a tree with their books, studying, while the grown-ups go ashore for water. Remember that tree. For days we've been in the cold north, with monks, islands and harps. Today the map swings far to the south. A teacher from the city of Tyre is sailing home with two young relatives, Frumentius and his brother Aedesius. The ship puts in at a harbor. And the people there, the old account says, are at odds with the Romans. They attack, and everyone on the ship is killed, except two boys found under a tree, reading.
screen: `A SHIP PUTS IN AT A HARBOR.`

segments.voice: The story is told by Rufinus, a church historian who says he heard it from Aedesius himself, years later. The boys are taken to the king. The king likes them. Aedesius becomes his cupbearer. Frumentius, the sharper of the two, is put in charge of the royal records and accounts. Then the king dies. He leaves a young son, and before he dies he sets the two foreigners free. They could go home. But the queen asks them to stay and help run the kingdom until the prince is grown, and they do. Frumentius uses his position quietly. He looks for Christian merchants passing through from the Roman world, and helps them set up places to meet and pray. When the prince comes of age, the brothers hand everything back and leave. Aedesius goes home to Tyre. Frumentius goes to Alexandria, to the bishop there, Athanasius, and says: there are Christians in that land, and they need a bishop. Athanasius listens, and answers, in effect: who could we find better than you? He makes Frumentius a bishop and sends him straight back. The old writers call the place India, a word they used loosely. Historians connect it with the kingdom of Aksum, in what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea. Ethiopian Christians remember Frumentius as their own, and call him Abba Salama, father of peace. And now the carry. In the Ethiopian Orthodox church, the altar holds a tabot, a tablet that stands for the tablets of the covenant kept in the ark. Ethiopian tradition says the ark itself rests in Ethiopia. So a church of the ark, begun with two boys under a tree.

Here's the practice: learn one fact about Ethiopia. You've already learned a few today: Abba Salama, the tabot on the altar, the ark the tradition speaks of. Settle, and breathe. Choose the one that stays with you. Hold it the way you'd hold a small, unfamiliar object someone handed you, turning it over, noticing it. Then let your mind go to the people who carry that fact every day as their own, in Ethiopia and wherever Ethiopians live now. If you pray, you can pray for them. If you don't, just hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Frumentius. The boy who survived a massacre in Ethiopia, served a king, stayed to help a queen, and came back as a bishop. Abba Salama.
Your line: the church of the ark. Today, look up one more thing about Ethiopia's church, or its people, that you didn't know this morning. Day seven hundred ninety-five.

796.title: Armenia (301)
796.hook: a kingdom turns to Christ through Gregory the Illuminator, after years in a pit
796.howItsDone: The Armenian Apostolic Church traces its roots to the apostles Thaddeus and Bartholomew and honors Saint Gregory the Illuminator as the one who brought the faith to the kingdom and as its first chief bishop; Armenian Catholics honor him too, and pilgrims visit the monastery at Khor Virap, built over the pit where tradition says he was held.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Frumentius, the boy under the tree who came back a bishop. Your line was the church of the ark. What did you learn about Ethiopia? Day seven hundred ninety-six.

A man in the king's service is told to honor the king's goddess, and he says no. He's a Christian. So the king has him thrown into a deep pit under a royal fortress, and leaves him there in the dark. Up above, time goes by and people forget him. The king assumes he's long dead. But in the way the Armenian story is told, one person hasn't forgotten: a woman who comes to the edge and keeps him alive with food let down into the dark. Today, the man in the pit, and the kingdom that came looking for him.

The man's name is Gregory, and the story comes from the old Armenian history that goes under the name of Agathangelos. The king is Tiridates. While Gregory is in the pit, the king does worse things. A group of Christian women, fleeing, come to Armenia, and when one of them, Hripsime, refuses the king, he has them killed. Then, the history says, the king is struck down, his mind broken, living like a wild animal. His sister has a dream, more than once: only Gregory can heal him. Everyone is sure Gregory is dead. They go to the pit anyway, lower a rope, and call down. And a voice answers. They pull him out, thin and blackened, but alive. Gregory goes to the king, and the king is healed. Gregory gathers the bones of the women who were killed and buries them with honor. He preaches, and the king who threw him in the pit is baptized. In the Armenian telling, this is the moment the kingdom turned to Christ. Tradition points to the place, and pilgrims still go there: Khor Virap, the deep pit. And Armenians gave Gregory a name: the Illuminator, the one who brought light. There's a line in the Psalms that fits him almost too well, in the old King James words: "He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock." Light came up out of a hole in the ground.

Here's the practice: hold Armenia in mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people of Armenia, and Armenians living far from it, wherever they are, carrying their own church and their own alphabet with them. You don't need to know much. Just picture a family at a table, a church on a hill, a grandmother lighting a candle. Then let your mind rest on anyone you know who is in a pit right now, the kind no one else sees. If you pray, you can pray for Armenia, and for them. If you don't, just hold them in the light for this sit. The bell holds the time.
Armenia. The kingdom whose story turns on a man in a pit, pulled out alive, who became Gregory the Illuminator.
Your line: light from a pit. Today, get something good to someone in a hard place: a message, a meal, a call. Day seven hundred ninety-six.

797.title: Thomas Christians
797.hook: Christians in Kerala trace their church to the apostle Thomas
797.howItsDone: The Thomas Christians of Kerala keep the memory of the apostle Thomas in their churches, feasts and songs, and their worship belongs to the Syriac tradition of the Christian East.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Armenia, and your line was light from a pit. Gregory came up out of the dark, and a kingdom changed. Where did you see a little light come out of a hard place? Day seven hundred ninety-seven.

"Let us also go, that we may die with him." That's Thomas, in John's Gospel. Jesus has decided to head back toward Judea, where people had just tried to stone him, and the other disciples are hesitating. Thomas says, in effect, fine, then we all go. Later, the same Thomas refuses to believe that Jesus is risen until he can touch the wounds, and the nickname sticks: doubting Thomas. But on the southwest coast of India, in Kerala, there are Christians who remember him differently. To them he's the apostle who came all the way to their shore. Today's word is the name they carry.

Start with what the Bible says, and what it doesn't. The book of Acts names Thomas among the apostles praying together in Jerusalem after the ascension. After that, the New Testament is silent about him. It never says where he went. Later writers filled the silence. A book called the Acts of Thomas, which is not part of the Bible, tells it like a folk tale. The apostles divide the world between them, and India falls to Thomas. He doesn't want to go. So, in the story, the risen Jesus sells him to a merchant as a carpenter, and off he goes. An Indian king hands him money to build a palace. Thomas gives it all to the poor, and when the king demands to see his palace, the answer is that it's being built in heaven. The historian Eusebius records a different tradition, that Thomas was sent to Parthia, the land of the Persians. So the old voices don't agree on the map, but they agree on the direction: east. And in Kerala, the Christians who call themselves Thomas Christians hold that he landed on their coast, preached, founded churches, and died a martyr in India. That's their tradition, kept in their own memory and in churches named for him. Historians weigh it differently, and the texts alone can't settle it. And notice who tradition sends to the far edge. Not the one with the keys. The one the nickname calls the doubter. The same Thomas who, when he finally saw the wounds, said the words in the King James Bible: "My Lord and my God." On this path, the story has mostly headed west, to Rome and beyond. Here is a thread running the other way.
screen: then, large: `MY LORD AND MY GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: settle, and let your breath slow down. Bring India to mind. If you've seen pictures of Kerala, let them come. If not, just hold the name. Christians there live alongside neighbors of other faiths, and they belong to more than one church. If you pray, you can pray for the church in India, by name, and for its neighbors too. If you don't pray, hold them in mind for a while and wish them peace. The bell holds the time.
Thomas Christians. The Christians of Kerala, in India, who trace their church back to the apostle Thomas.
Your line: thomas went east. Today, find Kerala on a map, down on India's southwest coast, and trace the distance back to Jerusalem with your finger. Day seven hundred ninety-seven.

798.title: The Xi'an stele (781)
798.hook: a stone in China records the luminous religion brought by Syriac-speaking monks
798.howItsDone: Christians of the Assyrian Church of the East and related churches remember the monks who carried their faith along the Silk Road, and the Xi'an stele is studied and visited as a record of that history.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Thomas Christians of Kerala, and your line was thomas went east. Did you find Kerala on the map? Today the road keeps going east. Day seven hundred ninety-eight.

A tall slab of dark stone stands in a museum in Xi'an, in China. It rests on the back of a carved stone tortoise. At the top, carved small, there's a cross, rising out of clouds and a lotus flower. Below it, columns of Chinese characters run down the face, and along the bottom and edges there's a second script, Syriac, the language of the churches of the East. The Chinese title calls it a memorial to the spread of the luminous religion in China. The stone tells how a teaching came east to China, carried by monks with books. Today's word is the stone.

Here's the story the stone tells, in paraphrase. A monk named Alopen came from the West, from a land the Chinese called Daqin, carrying scriptures and images. He arrived at the capital, Chang'an, the city we now call Xi'an. The emperor Taizong sent an official to welcome him, had his scriptures translated in the palace library, questioned him about the teaching, and then issued a decree allowing it to be taught. Monasteries were built. The stone then gives a summary of the faith, and this is the part that rewards slow reading. It speaks of one true God, of the Messiah born of a virgin, of a bright star announcing the birth, and of Persians who saw it and came with gifts. That's the wise men, told in Chinese. It speaks of baptism by water and of the cross. And it does all this in words borrowed from the religious language already living in China, some of it Buddhist, some Daoist. The monks didn't invent a new vocabulary. They reached for the words people already prayed with. Even the name they chose, the luminous teaching, is a word about light. The stone also records hard times, when the community was mocked and opposed, and then times of renewed favor. It was carved later than Alopen's arrival, as a look back on what had grown. The monks belonged to the Church of the East, and this stone lets that church speak for itself, in two scripts. This week the path has gone a long way: Caedmon singing after a dream in the stable, Cuthbert by the sea, Bede finishing his work, then Ethiopia, Armenia, Kerala, and now China. The church of these centuries was not one place. It was many roads.

Here's the practice: look at a map of the Silk Road. If you have your phone, search for one now and keep it in front of you. If not, draw one in your mind: the Mediterranean on the left, China on the right, and in between, deserts, mountains, oasis towns, Persia, Central Asia. Settle, and breathe. Follow the line with your eyes or your finger, slowly, from west to east, the way a monk with books and a walking stick might have gone. Notice how long it is. If you pray, you can pray for the Christians who live along that road today, and for everyone else who lives there too. The bell holds the time.
Xi'an stele. A carved stone in China that tells how monks of the Church of the East brought the luminous teaching to the emperor's capital.
